transcript.content: Hello, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, it’s good to meet you too. Um, so I came in today because... well, honestly, it’s been going on for months and I’ve really been trying to just tough it out on my own, but I literally feel like I’m crawling out of my skin. 

I’m taking some college classes right now and working as a tech in a radiology suite, and both of those things require a lot of just... sitting. Like, in the suite, when a scan is running or you're waiting on a doctor to read an image, you're just supposed to sit quietly at the computer console. But I can't do it. I mean, I try, I really do, but I just end up shifting around in my chair a million times, or my leg is bouncing, or I just flat-out have to stand up and start pacing around the control room. I'll even find some completely random excuse to move, like pretending I need to go double-check the lead aprons or restock something down the hall, just because I physically cannot stay seated. 

And it’s the exact same thing in my lectures. I just sit there feeling this intense need to move, and no matter how much I tell myself to just chill out and sit still like everyone else, I just can't. After months of trying to just push through it, I'm still pacing, still shifting, still looking for any excuse to get up. It’s just... it's exhausting, honestly, and I just can't keep trying to force it anymore, you know?
When you’re trying to sit still, do you get an uncomfortable feeling in your legs that makes you feel like you have to move them?

Um, no, not exactly? Like, it’s not really a physical discomfort or a weird sensation in my legs specifically. I know what you mean, like that creepy-crawly feeling some people get, but it’s definitely not that. My legs don't hurt or tingle or feel heavy or anything. 

It’s honestly more like... well, it’s like my whole body is just humming, you know? Like an engine that’s revving way too high but the car is in park. So my leg bounces—like, it bounces a *lot*, honestly it probably drives my coworkers and the other students crazy—but it’s not because my leg itself feels bad or uncomfortable. It’s just that the energy has to go *somewhere*. If I try to force my leg to stop bouncing, then I’ll just start tapping my pen, or shifting my weight back and forth, or drumming my fingers on the console desk. 

It’s this intense, full-body pressure where my brain is just screaming at me to do something, anything, other than just sit there. I'll be staring at the monitor, trying to wait for the radiologist to finish dictating an exam, and I'm just hyper-aware of how still I'm supposed to be, and that just makes the feeling even worse. It's like a tightly coiled spring inside my chest, not my legs. But yeah, no, to answer your question, it's not an uncomfortable feeling in my legs themselves. It's just a general, overwhelming urge to be in motion that I physically cannot ignore, no matter how hard I try to just lock myself into the chair.
Did this start after you began taking any new medication or using any drug?

No, no, I haven't started anything new. I mean, I take ibuprofen sometimes if I get a headache from staring at the screens too long in the radiology suite, because those monitors are super bright and the room is always kept so dark, you know? But other than that, no new medications, no prescription drugs, definitely no recreational stuff or anything like that. I don't even really drink coffee because honestly, I feel like I already have way too much caffeine running through my veins naturally, so I don't need to add to it. 

I've just been dealing with this on my own, completely unmedicated. And it's not like a sudden thing that just popped up overnight after taking a pill, it's just been this constant, steady build-up of feeling like I'm going to explode if I don't move. I keep thinking back, trying to pinpoint if there was some specific trigger, like maybe the stress of juggling college and the hospital job, but honestly, it's just been this escalating thing for months now. So yeah, definitely not related to any new medication or drug or anything like that. I wish it was that simple, to be honest, because then I could just stop taking whatever it was and go back to normal, but unfortunately, it's not.
When this happens, do you feel anxious?

Anxious? I mean... I don't think so? Like, I'm not sitting there worrying about things, you know? It's not like my heart is pounding because I'm scared I'm going to fail my classes or because I'm worried about messing up a scan at work. I mean, obviously, I don't want to mess up a scan, but I know how to do my job. It's not a fear thing. 

It's more just... frustration, maybe? Like, I get so frustrated that I can't just be normal and sit there like everyone else. I'll look over at the other techs and they're just chilling, scrolling on their phones or whatever while we wait for the radiologist, and I'm practically vibrating out of my chair. And then I start getting annoyed with myself, like, 'Dude, just stop moving, it's not that hard.' But it *is* that hard. 

So, I wouldn't call it anxiety. My mind isn't racing with all these terrible worst-case scenarios or anything. It's just that physical feeling of being trapped in a chair when my body is telling me I absolutely have to be up and doing something. I guess maybe it looks like anxiety from the outside because I'm fidgeting so much, but inside, I'm not panicking. I'm just incredibly restless and, honestly, just really tired of fighting it all day long.
Since you were a child, have you generally been someone who felt constantly on the go or had trouble staying seated?

Oh, wow, yeah. Like, absolutely. It's funny you ask about when I was a kid because my parents still bring it up all the time. Like, literally, every time we have a family dinner and someone mentions school or work, my mom will launch into this whole story about my elementary school parent-teacher conferences. She says it was like clockwork—every single year, the teachers would sit them down in those tiny little chairs and be like, "He's a smart kid, but he just cannot stay in his seat." 

And it wasn't just getting up, either. I was apparently the kid who was always blurting things out, calling out the answers before the teacher even finished asking the question, or just rushing ahead on assignments before they even finished explaining the directions. Like, I’d have the worksheet half done while everyone else was still listening to what we were supposed to do, but of course, I’d do it wrong because I didn't wait to hear the instructions. 

So, yeah, this is definitely not a new thing. It’s not like I just suddenly got restless because I’m balancing college classes and my radiology training and everything. I mean, the hospital environment is fast-paced, sure, but this feeling of having a motor running inside me? That’s been there forever. Way before middle school, way before high school. It’s like I’ve always been this way, just constantly on the go, moving from one thing to the next, never really able to just sit and be still. Even when I was a little kid playing with toys, I was never the one sitting quietly in the corner; I was running around the house, crashing into things, turning everything into some kind of high-speed race. So, yeah, definitely a lifelong thing for me.

latest_inference.note: Lifelong pattern since childhood of being 'on the go,' unable to stay seated, blurting out answers, and rushing tasks strongly supports ADHD; anxiety and substance/medication-induced causes are less likely, and the absence of leg discomfort plus childhood onset argues against restless legs or akathisia.
